patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 3,483 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2013: suspension: DR Congo suspends exit permits for children adopted by foreigners (25 September 2013) 2014: advisory: US State Dept strongly recommends against adopting from DR Congo (6 October 2014) 2016: law: DR Congo law preventing adoptions to the US takes effect (15 July 2016, per US FY2024 report)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004). Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders. Also home country of accused personnel: DR Congo → CAR: MINUSCA FARDC contingent allegations (offenders).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009). DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024). Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers. Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children.
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004); DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024); DR Congo — UN Mapping Report: rape of girls and of child soldiers in military camps by all forces (1993–2003); UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005); UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024; DR Congo — forced labour and sexual exploitation of children at eastern artisanal mines (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
cases.what: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.

cases.title: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC/FPLC)
cases.what: On 14 March 2012 the ICC found Thomas Lubanga guilty of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him on 10 July 2012 to 14 years; the verdict was confirmed on 1 December 2014. Sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but not charged. He was released on 15 March 2020 after serving his sentence.

cases.title: DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024)
cases.who: M23 (68), CODECO (63), FARDC (47), Raia Mutomboki, Nyatura, ADF and others
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC in 2024, by M23 (68), CODECO (63), the Armed Forces of the DRC (47), Raia Mutomboki (33), Nyatura (24) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, by ADF (265), M23 (178) and others. In 2022 it verified sexual violence against 284 children aged 4 to 17, 56 of them by FARDC.

cases.title: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
cases.who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
cases.what: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cover_up: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action

cases.title: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
cases.who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
cases.what: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.

cases.title: DR Congo — UN Mapping Report: rape of girls and of child soldiers in military camps by all forces (1993–2003)
cases.who: All parties: FAC (later FARDC), RCD-G, MLC, RCD-K/ML, RCD-N, UPC and PUSIC, FNI and FRPI, FAPC, Mayi-Mayi, ex-FAR/Interahamwe and others
cases.what: The UN human rights office's Mapping Exercise report, published on 1 October 2010, covered the most serious violations in DR Congo between 1993 and 2003. It described 'the apparent systematic use of rape and sexual assault allegedly by all combatant forces' against women and girls, including Hutu refugee children in 1996–97, and the widespread use of child soldiers by all parties, who suffered murder, rape and torture in military camps. It listed 12 parties named by the Secretary-General for recruiting children, among them the national army.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

cases.title: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army commanders Lt. Col. Binansio Okumu ('Binany') and 'Obol', reporting to Gen. Dominic Ongwen (per HRW)
cases.what: From 14 to 17 December 2009 Lord's Resistance Army forces attacked at least 10 villages in the remote Makombo area of Haute-Uélé, north-eastern DR Congo, killing at least 321 civilians and abducting 250 others, including at least 80 children. Human Rights Watch, which documented the previously unreported massacre after a field mission in February 2010, said it was carried out by two LRA commanders who reported to Gen. Dominic Ongwen, the senior LRA leader believed to command its forces in Congo and wanted by the International Criminal Court.

cases.title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

cases.title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.

cases.title: DR Congo — forced labour and sexual exploitation of children at eastern artisanal mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Mining bosses, miners, family members, government officials, armed groups
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says mining bosses, other miners, family members, government officials and armed groups force or coerce adults and children into forced labour in artisanal mines in eastern DRC, including through debt bondage, and that most trafficking is internal, including sex trafficking and forced marriage of girls.
cases.cover_up: Traffickers named in the report include government officials; corruption and complicity contributed to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2018: National Assembly AAMPETRA commission on sexual violence in schools (2017–2018).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Ecuador — National Assembly 'AAMPETRA' commission on sexual violence in schools (2018)
cases.who: Teachers and staff of public and private schools; Ministry of Education
cases.what: Ecuador's National Assembly set up a multiparty occasional commission in 2017 after families of pupils abused at the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari (AAMPETRA) in Quito, where 41 children were abused, mobilised. It reviewed cases from 2013 to 2017 and, in a report approved unanimously on 16 February 2018, found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities and concluded that former ministers had not acted. Human Rights Watch's later analysis of government data counted 4,221 pupils who suffered sexual violence in schools between 2014 and May 2020.
cases.cover_up: Commission found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities

cases.title: Ecuador — 103 complaints of sexual violence against clergy (Ecuavisa)
cases.who: Catholic clergy in Ecuador
cases.what: A months-long investigation by Ecuavisa's Visión 360 counted 103 complaints of sexual abuse involving Ecuadorian clergy, with cases in Guayas, Pichincha, Azuay and Los Ríos, including those of Fr César Cordero and Fr Luis Intriago. A survivors' association demanded that such crimes be made imprescriptible, as approved in a referendum.
cases.cover_up: Victims' families said the church hierarchy refused to share information or file complaints with prosecutors itself, contrary to a National Assembly commission report on sexual violence against children in education.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Iain Wares: Edinburgh → South Africa; Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson; Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore; Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander; England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Jimmy Savile: first report 1958, first action 2012 (54 years). Two police investigations in his lifetime (earliest 1958) produced no charges; Surrey Police 2007-09 dropped; BBC Newsnight report shelved Dec 2011; press inquiries from 1973 never published Cyril Smith MP: first report 1968, first action 2012 (44 years). A pupil told police in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; investigations in 1970, 1998, 1999 brought no charge; CPS said in 2012 he should have been charged over 40 years earlier Rotherham grooming networks: first report 1999, first action 2010 (11 years). Children's-home managers and Risky Business youth workers reported from the early-to-mid 1990s; researcher Angie Heal warned officials 2002-2007; a rape reported in 2001 led to release without charge Rochdale grooming ring: first report 2008, first action 2012 (4 years). A victim went to police in 2008 but the CPS declined to prosecute citing her credibility; NHS worker Sara Rowbotham's alerts were ignored; GMP apologised in 2015 for 2008-2010 failures Barry Bennell (English football): first report 1989, first action 1994 (5 years). A parent's anonymous letter to Crewe manager Dario Gradi (1989-90) asked for an investigation; the club kept him on with restrictions Kincora Boys' Home: first report 1977, first action 1980 (3 years). Allegations reached the RUC in 1977 and a report went to the DPP naming prominent businessmen, but no prosecution followed until press exposure; claims of MI5 protection were examined by the HIA inquiry, which found no state collusion Peter Ball (Bishop of Gloucester): first report 1992, first action 2015 (23 years). Cautioned in 1993 and resigned, but continued to officiate; Lambeth Palace received seven supportive letters in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating to police (IICSA) John Smyth QC: first report 1982, first action 2017 (35 years). The 1982 Ruston Report described the beatings; the Makin Review (2024) found a cover-up by "powerful evangelical clergy"; Archbishop Justin Welby, told in 2013, took no action and resigned 12 Nov 2024 Fr Brendan Smyth (Norbertines): first report 1975, first action 1991 (16 years). At a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; moved between parishes and countries; RUC extradition request mishandled by the Irish Attorney General's office Greville Janner: first report 1991, first action 2015 (24 years). Police investigated in 1991, 2002, 2007 without charges; Henriques report (2016) said a prosecution would likely have succeeded
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Scotland 2017: Limitation (Childhood Abuse) (Scotland) Act 2017 removed the three-year time bar for childhood abuse civil claims (announced in force 4 Oct 2017) England and Wales 2026: Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.96 removed the three-year limitation period for child sexual abuse personal-injury claims, retrospectively; in force 29 June 2026; defendants must show a fair trial is impossible
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2003: Sexual Offences Act 2003 allows prosecution in England, Wales and NI of offences against children abroad (Scotland: 1995 Act); used to convict Richard Huckle in 2016 2019: Europol IOCTA 2019: live distant child abuse (LDCA) is the most common form of commercial child sexual exploitation; the Philippines remains the most prominent victim location; some offenders also travel; EU police urged to use PNR travel data
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role_note: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity (investigated and disproved). Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims (investigated and disproved). Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims (investigated and disproved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role_note: United Kingdom → Philippines demand for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'; Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings; Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA; Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA; Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff; Islington Council children's homes, London; Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales); British child migration programmes — IICSA; Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC); Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals; Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale; IICSA Westminster report — deference and failures (no proven 'VIP ring'); Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire children's homes; never tried; Rotherham — IOPC Operation Linden report on South Yorkshire Police (2022.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity. Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims. Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims. UK government study of 'satanic ritual abuse' claims — La Fontaine report (1994).
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff
cases.who: Medomsley Detention Centre for young offenders (Home Office Prison Service)
cases.what: Medomsley held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, an officer who ran the kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and again in 2005 and died in 2010; the Ombudsman called him 'possibly the most prolific sex offender in British history'. Operation Seabrook (from 2013) identified 32 living suspects; five former officers were convicted in 2019 and another in 2023, eight former staff jailed in total. The Ombudsman's report of 12 November 2025, based on 8,000 documents and 74 witnesses, found the authorities failed in their duty to keep detainees safe.
cases.cover_up: The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman (November 2025) found that knowledge of the abuse held by the Prison Service, police and Home Office was 'ignored and dismissed', families' complaints led to no action, and successive wardens were 'either complicit or incompetent'.

cases.title: Operation Stovewood — NCA Rotherham investigation
cases.who: National Crime Agency investigation into non-recent exploitation in Rotherham
cases.what: The National Crime Agency took over the Rotherham investigation in 2014. Its page reports about 1,150 potential victims identified, more than 220 people arrested or interviewed voluntarily, and 39 people convicted with about 470 years of prison sentences. On 8 August 2025 the NCA agreed to take over an investigation, directed by the Independent Office for Police Conduct, into allegations of child sexual abuse by former South Yorkshire Police officers (allegations; no finding yet).

cases.title: Newcastle — Operation Sanctuary
cases.who: Grooming networks; Northumbria Police
cases.what: Operation Sanctuary began in 2014 and led to 18 people being jailed for sexually abusing girls and young women they had groomed in Newcastle. The Joint Serious Case Review, published 23 February 2018, put the number of victims at about 700 across the Northumbria area, 108 of them in Newcastle. It found no evidence that concerns about political correctness or accusations of racism made police reluctant to investigate, and called for law changes on sexual exploitation.

cases.title: Barry Bennell and English youth football (Sheldon Review)
cases.who: Barry Bennell (coach/scout, Crewe Alexandra, Manchester City links); The Football Association
cases.what: Bennell was first jailed in Florida in 1994 for raping a British boy on a football tour, then received prison sentences in Britain in 1998, 2015, February 2018 (50 offences against 12 boys aged eight to 14, 1979–1990; 30 years) and October 2020 (a fifth sentence, making 34 years in total). After a former player spoke out publicly in November 2016, BBC News reported within weeks that 350 people had alleged they were victims, linked to 55 clubs. Clive Sheldon QC's review for the FA (17 Mar 2021) recorded at least 240 suspects and 692 survivors across football, said the true numbers were likely far higher, found the FA had acted 'far too slowly' on child protection, and criticised Manchester City, Crewe and Stoke over Bennell. Bennell died in prison in September 2023.
cases.cover_up: Crewe Alexandra heard an allegation but kept Bennell on with restrictions (former director Hamilton Smith). The Sheldon Review found the FA guilty of 'institutional failure' for delaying safeguards after 1995.

cases.title: Oxford — Operation Bullfinch and 2015 Serious Case Review
cases.who: Grooming network; Thames Valley Police; Oxfordshire County Council
cases.what: Seven men were jailed in May 2013 for a combined minimum of 95 years after Operation Bullfinch; the trial judge said police and social services missed tell-tale signs. The Oxfordshire Serious Case Review, published 3 March 2015, estimated that more than 350 young people were sexually exploited in the county from 1999 to 2014. It found police did not believe the girls and treated them as if they had chosen their situation, and social services knew of grooming but failed to protect them. Both the police and council apologised.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
cases.cover_up: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.

cases.title: 'Kids the Light of our Lives' forum
cases.who: Online chat forum with live streaming of abuse
cases.what: An internet chat room, hosted from Buxhall in Suffolk, featuring images and live streams of the sexual abuse of children. Forensic teams found 75,960 indecent images on the host's computer and evidence he had supplied 11,491 images to other users. The trail began in Canada with the arrest of 24 offenders; in a 10-month operation by the Virtual Global Taskforce, led by the UK's CEOP and involving agencies from 35 countries, officers posed as the host and ran the chat room for 10 days. British authorities said on 18 June 2007 that more than 700 suspects had been identified worldwide and 31 children rescued, some only a few months old. The host, Timothy David Martyn Cox, admitted nine counts of possessing and distributing indecent images and was given an indeterminate sentence at Ipswich Crown Court that day.

cases.title: Derby — Operation Retriever
cases.who: Grooming network; Derbyshire Police investigation
cases.what: Derbyshire Police's Operation Retriever led to the conviction of nine men in 2010 for grooming and sexually abusing 26 girls, one aged 12. Thirteen men had been charged and eleven stood trial.

cases.title: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
cases.who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
cases.what: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.
cases.cover_up: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.

cases.title: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
cases.who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
cases.what: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing thousands of child abuse images (about 4,000; jailed four months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002 amid sex-crime allegations. In March 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11; he spent about two and a half years in jail there. In February 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape, four indecent assaults and one count of sex with a girl under 13, against three girls in 1975–1980, and sentenced to 16 years. Released in February 2023, he was recalled to prison in March 2023 for breaching licence conditions.

cases.title: Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor
cases.who: Ghislaine Maxwell
cases.what: Maxwell was arrested on 2 July 2020 in Bradford, New Hampshire. On 29 December 2021 a jury convicted her on five of six counts, including sex trafficking of a minor; she was acquitted of enticing a minor to travel. She was sentenced on 28 June 2022 to 20 years. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction on 17 Sept 2024 and the US Supreme Court declined her appeal on 6 Oct 2025; she had argued Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement shielded co-conspirators. As of mid-2026 her lawyer said he would seek a pardon; Blanche said in May 2026 he would not recommend one.
cases.cover_up: In July 2025 Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche interviewed Maxwell with limited immunity; on 1 Aug 2025 she was moved to the minimum-security Federal Prison Camp Bryan, Texas. A DOJ official recorded secretly said the transfer was against policy (DOJ said he had no role).

cases.title: Halifax/Calderdale — West Yorkshire grooming trials
cases.who: Grooming networks; West Yorkshire Police
cases.what: On 6 November 2024, 20 men were jailed for more than 200 years combined for raping and abusing four girls aged 12 to 16 in Calderdale between 2001 and 2010, after three West Yorkshire Police investigations. In May 2026 six more men were convicted over the abuse of one girl from 2006 to 2009, which she reported to police in 2019.

cases.title: Fr Paul Moore — moved by his bishop to Toronto
cases.who: Diocese of Galloway; Bishop Maurice Taylor
cases.what: Fr Francis 'Paul' Moore was found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow in 2018 of abusing three boys in Ayrshire in the 1970s and indecently assaulting a student priest in 1995, and was jailed for nine years. He had confessed his attraction to boys to Bishop Maurice Taylor of Galloway in 1996; Taylor sent him to a treatment centre in Toronto and to Fort Augustus Abbey, removed him from ministry but let him live in a church-bought house, and did not report him.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore to Toronto and Fort Augustus

cases.title: Keighley — 2016 convictions
cases.who: Grooming network
cases.what: In February 2016 twelve men were jailed, with sentences of up to 20 years, for sexually exploiting a vulnerable teenage girl in Keighley. A further six men were jailed in 2022 for the systematic rape of another teenage girl in the town.

cases.title: Operation Yewtree — post-Savile investigation of public figures
cases.who: Metropolitan Police
cases.what: Launched by the Metropolitan Police on 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations, Yewtree had arrested 19 people by October 2015. Those convicted include Paul Gadd (Gary Glitter), Max Clifford, Rolf Harris, former DJ Chris Denning, Dave Lee Travis (one count, involving an adult) and, in April 2017, ex-BBC worker Geoffrey Wheeler, which the BBC called the operation's sixth conviction; Stoke Mandeville doctor Michael Salmon was also convicted in 2015 after a Yewtree investigation. Others were acquitted or never charged, including several well-known names, and must not be described as offenders.

flows.what: Sri Lankan children adopted to United Kingdom in the 1980s (baby-farm period).

flows.title: UK → Australia child migrants
flows.what: Children in British care were sent to institutions in Australia where IICSA found a catalogue of evidence of ill-treatment and sexual abuse; the last child was migrated in 1970.

flows.what: British child migration to Canada began in the 19th century; IICSA found the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its schools in Canada.

flows.what: New Zealand's Social Development Minister said in November 2009 that 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954 and that most were placed in foster care rather than institutions; IICSA lists New Zealand among the destinations of British child migration.

flows.what: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.

flows.title: Gary Glitter: UK → Cambodia → Vietnam
flows.what: After his 1999 UK conviction, Paul Gadd moved to Cambodia (expelled 2002–03) and then Vietnam, where he was convicted in 2006 of obscene acts with girls aged 10 and 11.

flows.title: Iain Wares: Edinburgh → South Africa
flows.what: Fettes College dismissed teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial; he went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children. South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025.

flows.title: United Kingdom → Philippines demand for livestreamed abuse
flows.what: IJM UK states the UK is among the top three global consumers of livestreamed abuse of Filipino children.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in Bulgaria (IWF 2025)
flows.what: Bulgaria hosted 87,959 URLs actioned by IWF in 2025, up from 9% share in 2024, driven by 'just a few particular sites'.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in the United States (IWF 2025)
flows.what: US hosting services held 49,021 URLs actioned by IWF in 2025.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Jeffrey Epstein and associates
networks.what: Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.

networks.name: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
networks.what: Savile used his BBC celebrity and NHS fundraising roles to gain access to children and patients for decades. Inquiries found 72 victims linked to the BBC (Smith, 2016) and victims aged 5–75 across NHS sites (Lampard, 2015); the Met recorded 214 crimes (2013).

networks.name: Operation Yewtree (UK entertainment figures)
networks.what: Metropolitan Police investigation opened 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations; 19 arrests and 7 convictions of entertainment figures.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

cases.title: Timor-Leste — Truth commission finds over 4,000 children taken to Indonesia, renamed and converted (2005)
cases.who: Indonesian military; Islamic and other organisations and individuals that took children
cases.what: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, in 2005, covering 1974 to 1999. It found that at least 4,000 children were forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the occupation, by military units, some of which used them as child soldiers or servants, and by Islamic organisations that converted them; children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. It called separating a child from their true identity, culture, religion or language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. CAVR and the joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, which was never created.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Indonesia — baby trafficking syndicate selling infants to Singapore
cases.who: Syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers
cases.what: In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some 'reserved while still in the womb', for 11–16 million rupiah each, after preparing fraudulent family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested and six babies about to be trafficked were rescued; police sought Interpol help to trace the adopters.

cases.title: Indonesia — child sexual exploitation in the Riau Islands and 'contract marriages' in Puncak (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign offenders; brokers of 'contract marriages'
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says extraterritorial child sexual exploitation is prevalent in the Riau Islands bordering Singapore, and women and girls are coerced into commercial sex notably in Batam. It also reports that Middle Eastern tourists pay more than $700 for week-long 'contract marriages' in Puncak, Bogor, involving girls as young as nine, a practice the government tacitly accepted. In October 2017 Batam police arrested a Singaporean man accused of molesting three boys (IBTimes, charged).
cases.cover_up: The report says the government tacitly accepted 'contract marriages'; corruption and complicity significantly impeded efforts.

networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2012: Iceland — Catholic Church investigative commission (Landakotsskóli).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 7,455 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Iceland — Catholic Church investigative commission on Landakotsskóli (2012)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Iceland; Landakotsskóli school and church summer camps
cases.what: An investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir, reported in early November 2012. It confirmed that Rev. Ágúst Georg, principal of the church's Landakotsskóli school, and teacher Margrét Müller abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse. It found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter reporting abuse by the priest. In December 2015 the Althing passed Act No. 117/2015, extending the state compensation scheme for abuse in institutions to Landakotsskóli.
cases.cover_up: The commission reported that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest had abused him.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Son Jong-woo, operator of Welcome to Video (2020): Freed after Korean sentence; 24 months more in July 2022 for concealing proceeds
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 18,578 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 1974: attempted halt: South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia; Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats sent nine pleas and it resumed 1989: policy: South Korea adopts policy to phase out intercountry adoption after peak of 8,837 in 1985 2012: law: Special Adoption Act takes effect (August), aiming to cut intercountry adoption 2022: inquiry: Truth and Reconciliation Commission opens investigation into overseas adoptions (December), after Danish Korean Rights Group petitions 2024: suspension: Sweden stops adoptions from South Korea 2025: finding: TRC finds state responsible for human rights violations in overseas adoptions (26 March); President Lee apologises (2 October)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2013: Korean Institute of Criminology (Jan 2013): South Korean men are the primary market for child sex tourism in Southeast Asia
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.
