patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses; South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption; Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case; South Korea — runaway children in commercial sex; police officer convicted (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
cases.who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
cases.what: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram chatrooms; at least 10,000 people used the 'Doctor's Room' chats, some paying up to $1,200. At least 74 victims, including 16 minors, were exploited there. After petitions signed by millions, police named the operator, Cho Ju-bin, in March 2020 — the first official identity disclosure for a sex offender in South Korea — and on 26 November 2020 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to 40 years (reported raised to 42 years on appeal in 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, who created the original 'Nth Room' chatrooms, was sentenced to 34 years by the Andong court on 8 April 2021. The law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.
cases.cover_up: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.

cases.title: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
cases.who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
cases.what: A 2005 investigation found that six people at the school, including the headmaster, had sexually harassed or raped at least nine deaf students from 2000 onward. Four received prison terms, two of which were later suspended; two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations had expired. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police opened a new investigation, the city moved to close the school in November 2011, and on 28 Oct 2011 the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for sexually assaulting an 18-year-old student in April 2005.
cases.cover_up: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: South Korea — runaway children in commercial sex; police officer convicted (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Entertainment establishments, escort services, chat-room operators
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit South Korean women and children, including runaways, in bars, nightclubs and internet-advertised escort services, and chat-room operators coerce children with compromising images into producing sexual material. A court convicted a local police officer in a 2022 case involving alleged complicity in trafficking-related crimes and sentenced him to five years; another officer was acquitted.
cases.cover_up: NGOs previously reported some local police sexually exploited children; one officer was convicted (bribery, secrecy violations) and another acquitted.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

cases.title: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
cases.who: French government and adoption associations
cases.what: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.
cases.cover_up: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.

cases.title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
cases.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
cases.what: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Denmark — Appeals Board finds 'systematic illegal behaviour' in Korean adoptions 1970–1989
cases.who: Danish adoption agencies DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp (and Terre des Hommes); South Korean agencies
cases.what: A report released in January 2024 by Denmark's Appeals Board (Ankestyrelsen), which supervises intercountry adoption, examined adoptions from South Korea between 1970 and 1989, when 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark. It found 'systematic illegal behaviour' on the Korean side: weak regulation let organisations alter adoptees' identities and backgrounds in official documents, and large sums of money passed between organisations in the two countries. It found that DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp knew about the changing of children's information. Adoptee groups said it did not examine the Danish state's role.
cases.cover_up: Two Danish agencies knew that children's information was being changed.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
cases.who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
cases.what: In August 2024 a journalist's reporting revealed Telegram chatrooms, some dedicated to specific high schools and middle schools, where users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female students, teachers and others; one room for pupils at a single school had more than 2,000 members. Within a week activists had identified more than 500 schools and universities as targets. Police said they had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024 by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, and that most victims and perpetrators were teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possessing or watching sexual deepfakes; earlier that month police opened an investigation into whether Telegram was complicit.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.
cases.cover_up: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.

cases.title: Senate 'Lost Innocents' — child migrants abused in Australian institutions (2001)
cases.who: Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia (Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf, Tardun) and other receiving institutions for British and Maltese child migrants
cases.what: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Lost Innocents: Righting the Record — Report on child migration' in August 2001. Of 207 former child migrants who made submissions, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.

cases.title: Malta — Church Response Team figures on clergy abuse 1991–2010
cases.who: Catholic Church in Malta — Response Team set up by the Maltese bishops (chair Judge Victor Caruana Colombo)
cases.what: In April 2010 the Maltese Curia said the Church's Response Team, set up by the bishops in 1991 and chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 remained open, four priests were found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. The convictions over St Joseph Home are already on the map.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Congregation of Christian Brothers
networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2015: Moss Review into allegations at the Nauru Regional Processing Centre.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. cases.title: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015)
cases.who: Australian-funded Regional Processing Centre on Nauru; contracted guards and staff
cases.what: The Moss Review, commissioned by the Australian government and published in March 2015, was aware of three rape allegations at the Australian-run Regional Processing Centre on Nauru, one involving a minor, confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child, and concluded that guards trading marijuana with detainees for sexual favours was possibly occurring. In April 2015 staff alleged multiple instances of sexual abuse of women and children in an open letter. A Senate select committee reported on 31 August 2015 in 'Taking responsibility: conditions and circumstances at Australia's Regional Processing Centre in Nauru'.
cases.cover_up: Staff wrote in an open letter in April 2015 that the Australian government had known of alleged abuses against women and children for more than 18 months

cases.title: Australia — 'The Forgotten Children': national inquiry into children in immigration detention
cases.who: Australian Government immigration detention (onshore centres and Nauru regional processing centre)
cases.what: The Australian Human Rights Commission's national inquiry, 'The Forgotten Children', was tabled in Federal Parliament on 11 February 2015. It reported 33 incidents of reported sexual assault in immigration detention between January 2013 and March 2014, 'the vast majority involving children'. A separate government-commissioned review by Philip Moss (March 2015) on the Nauru centre was aware of three rape allegations, one involving a minor, and confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Yemen — UN Group of Eminent Experts: rape of boys and girls by armed forces; sexual violence against recruited girls
cases.who: Security Belt Forces; Yemeni 35th Armoured Brigade; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa; Houthi de facto authorities
cases.what: The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 (A/HRC/42/17) that Security Belt Forces raped 18 women, four boys and a girl in 2016–2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden; members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy; and Houthi detention sites saw sexual violence against a 17-year-old boy. Its September 2020 report found credible accounts that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13–17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.

cases.title: Ethiopia — girls trafficked to Djibouti, Sudan and Saudi Arabia (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers and begging rings
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in forced begging, sometimes via organized begging rings, in Saudi Arabia, and exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs for control. Reports of official complicity continued.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Syria — abduction of children by armed groups and government forces (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. cases.title: Syria — abduction of children by armed groups and government forces (UN verified)
cases.who: Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, Syrian government forces, YPG/YPJ
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 14 children (5 boys, 9 girls) in Syria in 2024 by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement (9), Syrian government forces (4) and YPG/YPJ (1), often for recruitment and use.

cases.title: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
cases.who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
cases.what: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria; thousands remain missing.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Syria — UN Commission of Inquiry: rape of detained women, girls and boys; forced marriage of girls by ISIS (2018)
cases.who: Syrian government forces and affiliated militias (worst offenders); Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham; Islamic State
cases.what: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic released 'I lost my dignity' on 15 March 2018, based on 454 interviews covering March 2011 to December 2017. It found sexual and gender-based violence pervasive and committed by most parties: women and girls were raped in detention, at checkpoints and in house raids, and male detainees including boys were subjected to sexual torture, with government forces and allied militias named as the worst offenders. It found that Islamic State forced girls and women into marriages with its fighters, and that these acts amount to war crimes.

cases.title: Lebanon — Chez Maurice and Silver-B: about 75 Syrian women freed from sex-trafficking ring (2016)
cases.who: Chez Maurice and Silver-B brothels
cases.what: In March 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels, Chez Maurice and Silver-B, in the Maameltein red-light district of Jounieh, and arrested and indicted over a dozen people on sex-trafficking charges. HRW said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk and that the same premises had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found, and later reopened. Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims in 2016, mainly these survivors.
cases.cover_up: Chez Maurice was raided in late 2011 when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found trapped there, closed for about three months and reopened. A survivor told Legal Agenda a trafficker claimed he had 'bought the state'.

cases.title: Jordan and Türkiye — Syrian refugee girls in forced marriages and sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Families and brokers arranging unofficial marriages
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Syrian girls in Türkiye — which hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians — are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. In Jordan, Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages, and in 2022 authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.
cases.cover_up: Türkiye: no investigations of complicit officials reported, though corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.

flows.what: Captives were moved in buses and trucks to holding sites in Tal Afar and Mosul, then women and girls were transferred to Raqqa and sold.

flows.title: Syria → Lebanon (refugee women and girls into sex trafficking)
flows.what: Criminal groups recruit Syrian women and girls with false job offers and exploit them in Lebanese brothels; Syrian children held in bonded labour in the Beqaa.

networks.name: Islamic State (ISIS / Da'esh)
networks.what: ISIS abducted thousands of Yazidi women and children from Sinjar in August 2014 and ran markets for their sale; the UN COI found genocide. Affiliates in West Africa, the Sahel and Mozambique are verified by the UN as abducting children.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014); Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019); Scranton (USA) → Ciudad del Este (Paraguay): Fr Carlos Urrutigoity; Tehuacán → Los Angeles → Mexico: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera; Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth; Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson; Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Jeffrey Epstein: first report 1996, first action 2006 (10 years). Maria Farmer reported to the FBI in 1996 with no known action; after the 2005 Palm Beach police probe, the 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement ended the federal case and he served 13 months in a county stockade on a state plea (2008). Federal sex-trafficking charges came only in July 2019 after the Miami Herald series (2018) Larry Nassar: first report 1997, first action 2016 (19 years). Athletes complained from 1997, including to MSU coach Kathie Klages; USA Gymnastics told 17 June 2015 and FBI in July 2015, but the FBI did not act; DOJ IG (2021) found at least 70 more athletes abused between FBI reports and his arrest Jerry Sandusky (Penn State): first report 1998, first action 2011 (13 years). A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted; a 2001 eyewitness report by Mike McQueary went to Paterno and university leaders, who did not report to police (Freeh report, 2012) Theodore McCarrick: first report 1994, first action 2018 (24 years). A priest wrote to Bishop Hughes in 1994; the nuncio was warned in 1994; further warnings including to Benedict XVI (2008); McCarrick denied them to the Vatican and was made a cardinal in 2001 R. Kelly: first report 2000, first action 2019 (19 years). Chicago Sun-Times investigated from August 2000; 2002 child-pornography prosecution ended in acquittal in 2008 Mark Foley (House pages): first report 2000, first action 2006 (6 years). Complaints reached House staff and leaders 2000-2005; House Ethics Committee found Speaker Hastert and others "negligent" Jared Fogle: first report 2007, first action 2015 (8 years). Allegations surfaced 2007; a franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 Fr Gilbert Gauthe (Lafayette): first report 1974, first action 1985 (11 years). Made Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy 1976 and returned
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role: Lobbying against reform and bankruptcy filings
patterns.role_note: At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims; Catholic, insurance and Scouts lobbying against limitation reform is documented in several states.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington: Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 3,137 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved). Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.role_note: 2003: PROTECT Act (30 April 2003): US citizens/residents prosecutable for illicit sexual conduct abroad with under-18s whether or not they intended it before travel; maximum raised to 30 years. ICE "Operation Predator" (2003) led to over 11,000 arrests incl. more than 1,100 outside the US 2016: International Megan's Law signed 8 Feb 2016; from 31 Oct 2017 passports of covered offenders carry a unique identifier; 21-day advance notice of foreign travel; Angel Watch notifies destination countries
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days (police ran abuse sites to catch users). Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 49,021 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (16% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions; Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation; Los Angeles County juvenile halls and MacLaren Children's Center — $4bn settlement; New Hampshire Youth Development Center, Manchester; US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018; Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'; Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge; Epstein — 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 state plea; Epstein — 2019 federal sex-trafficking indictment and death in custody; Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor; Zorro Ranch, New Mexico — state probe dropped in 2019, reopened 2026; Epstein Files Transparency Act and DOJ releases (2025–2026); Larry Nassar — USA Gymnastics and Michigan State Unive.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Investigations have been state-level (attorneys general, grand juries) and church-commissioned
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska. 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria. McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

cases.title: Barry Bennell and English youth football (Sheldon Review)
cases.who: Barry Bennell (coach/scout, Crewe Alexandra, Manchester City links); The Football Association
cases.what: Bennell was first jailed in Florida in 1994 for raping a British boy on a football tour, then received prison sentences in Britain in 1998, 2015, February 2018 (50 offences against 12 boys aged eight to 14, 1979–1990; 30 years) and October 2020 (a fifth sentence, making 34 years in total). After a former player spoke out publicly in November 2016, BBC News reported within weeks that 350 people had alleged they were victims, linked to 55 clubs. Clive Sheldon QC's review for the FA (17 Mar 2021) recorded at least 240 suspects and 692 survivors across football, said the true numbers were likely far higher, found the FA had acted 'far too slowly' on child protection, and criticised Manchester City, Crewe and Stoke over Bennell. Bennell died in prison in September 2023.
cases.cover_up: Crewe Alexandra heard an allegation but kept Bennell on with restrictions (former director Hamilton Smith). The Sheldon Review found the FA guilty of 'institutional failure' for delaying safeguards after 1995.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Larry Nassar — USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University
cases.who: Larry Nassar (team doctor); USA Gymnastics; Michigan State University; FBI; US Olympic & Paralympic Committee
cases.what: Nassar pleaded guilty to federal child-abuse-image charges (60 years, Dec 2017) and to criminal sexual conduct in two Michigan counties, receiving 40–175 years in Ingham County (Jan 2018) and 40–125 years in Eaton County (Feb 2018); by the final hearing the number of identified victims had reached 265. Settlements: Michigan State University $500m to more than 300 women and girls (2018); USA Gymnastics and the USOPC $380m (2021); the US government $138.7m to 139 claimants over FBI failures to investigate promptly (April 2024). The Indianapolis Star's September 2016 investigation triggered the case.
cases.cover_up: Athletes complained as early as 1997. USAG was told on 17 June 2015. The DOJ Inspector General (July 2021) found FBI agents failed to act on the gymnasts' reports and that supervisory agent W. Jay Abbott later lied about it. MSU dean William Strampel was convicted of misconduct in office (2019); charges against ex-MSU president Lou Anna Simon (dismissed 2020) and ex-USAG CEO Steve Penny (dropped 2022) did not end in convictions; coach Kathie Klages's conviction was overturned (2021). USA Gymnastics had complaints against 54 coaches 1996–2006.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Samoa — Focus on Children (Utah) adoption fraud
cases.who: Focus on Children, Utah agency run by Scott and Karen Banks
cases.what: Samoan parents were told their children would go to the US temporarily for schooling, but the children were adopted permanently. A federal indictment on 28 February 2007 charged Scott and Karen Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. All pleaded guilty on 6 January 2009 to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of an alien, and the agency to a felony conspiracy; in February 2009 Judge David Sam sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
cases.cover_up: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.

cases.title: Operation Hamlet — parents sharing abuse of their own children
cases.who: International online network of offenders, many abusing their own children
cases.what: Danish National Police, acting on information from Save the Children about images found online, arrested a man and his wife who had posted images of the abuse of their nine-year-old daughter; from November 2001 the US Customs CyberSmuggling Center coordinated US inquiries with Danish police, INTERPOL and NCMEC. On 9 August 2002 US Customs announced 10 arrests of US citizens, with 10 more suspects arrested in Denmark, Belgium, Germany, England, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and 45 children rescued, 37 of them in the US; in many cases parents were abusing their own children. Fifteen suspects, five of them foreign nationals, were indicted on federal conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of California on 8 August 2002.

cases.title: Diocese of Lafayette — Gilbert Gauthe (first national case)
cases.who: Diocese of Lafayette; Fr Gilbert Gauthe
cases.what: Fr Gilbert Gauthe admitted abusing 37 children while serving in the Diocese of Lafayette from 1972 to 1983. In 1974 the bishop made him a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations about altar boys. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years; the diocese paid more than $20 million. His 1984–85 case was the first widely publicised clergy abuse prosecution in the US.
cases.cover_up: Bishop assigned him as Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy in 1976 and returned

cases.title: Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge
cases.who: Jeffrey Epstein (financier)
cases.what: In March 2005 a woman told Palm Beach police her 14-year-old stepdaughter had been paid to give Epstein a massage at his mansion. A 13-month police investigation identified about 35 girls. In July 2006 a state grand jury returned a single count of felony solicitation of prostitution and Epstein was arrested on 23 July 2006. Reiter later called the outcome 'the worst failure of the criminal justice system' in modern times.
cases.cover_up: Police chief Michael Reiter said state prosecutors under State Attorney Barry Krischer grew dismissive about six months in; he asked Krischer to step aside. The July 2006 state grand jury returned only one felony solicitation-of-prostitution count. Reiter then referred the case to the FBI.

cases.title: Epstein — 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 state plea
cases.who: Jeffrey Epstein; US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida (Alexander Acosta)
cases.what: After the FBI opened a federal probe, US Attorney Alexander Acosta's office negotiated a non-prosecution agreement in 2007. On 30 June 2008 Epstein pleaded guilty in Palm Beach County to soliciting prostitution and soliciting a minor; he was sentenced to 18 months, registered as a sex offender and was released on 22 July 2009 after 13 months. A 2018 Miami Herald series (Julie K. Brown) identified 80 victims and reopened scrutiny. Acosta resigned as US Labor Secretary in July 2019.
cases.cover_up: Lenient deal: the federal non-prosecution agreement (2007) dropped federal charges against Epstein and 'several suspected co-conspirators' in return for a state guilty plea; it was kept from victims. Epstein served 13 months of an 18-month term, much of it on daily work release. In Feb 2019 Judge Kenneth Marra ruled prosecutors violated the Crime Victims' Rights Act by not telling victims while urging them to 'have patience'. DOJ OPR (Nov 2020) found Acosta used 'poor judgment' but committed no professional misconduct; an 11-month gap in Acosta's incoming emails was noted.

cases.title: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
cases.who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
cases.what: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained trying to take 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic without proper documentation; their interpreters said group members had spoken with the children's parents. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association. In February a judge released eight, concluding they had not knowingly committed a crime, and later a ninth; the kidnapping and criminal association charges were dropped. On 17 May 2010 the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel under a 1980 law restricting movement out of Haiti and sentenced to the 3 months and 8 days she had already served.

cases.title: Jared Fogle (Subway spokesman) — child abuse material and paid sex with minors
cases.who: Jared Fogle; Russell Taylor (co-conspirator); Subway
cases.what: After his Indianapolis home was raided in July 2015 in a child abuse material investigation, Fogle pleaded guilty to receiving child abuse material and travelling to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor, and on 19 Nov 2015 was sentenced to 188 months (15 years 8 months). He had already paid $100,000 restitution to each of 14 victims ($1.4m); two were 16 and 17 when he travelled to have sex with them.
cases.cover_up: Allegations surfaced in 2007 but the FBI acted only in 2015. A franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 about Fogle's messages seeking sex with a minor; Subway says it has no record.

cases.title: Jerry Sandusky — Penn State football and The Second Mile
cases.who: Jerry Sandusky (assistant coach); Pennsylvania State University; The Second Mile charity
cases.what: Sandusky, a former Penn State assistant football coach, was charged in Nov 2011 and convicted in June 2012 of 45 counts of sexual abuse involving 10 boys, some assaulted on the Penn State campus; in Oct 2012 he was sentenced to 30–60 years. He met boys through The Second Mile charity he founded in 1977. The Freeh report (July 2012), commissioned by the university, found the most senior Penn State leaders showed 'total disregard' for the victims' safety. The NCAA fined Penn State $60m.
cases.cover_up: A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted. In 2001 graduate assistant Mike McQueary reported seeing Sandusky with a boy in a shower; it went to Joe Paterno, athletic director Tim Curley and vice-president Gary Schultz. The Freeh report (July 2012) found Paterno, president Graham Spanier, Curley and Schultz concealed Sandusky's activities. Curley, Schultz and Spanier were convicted of child endangerment in 2017.

cases.title: Samuel Bateman — FLDS splinter group, Short Creek
cases.who: Splinter group of the FLDS led by Samuel Bateman
cases.what: Samuel Bateman began claiming to be a new prophet in 2019 and led a group that broke off from the FLDS church. In a plea agreement he admitted 'spiritually marrying' 20 women and girls, 10 of them under age, with the intent of sexual activity with the girls. He was arrested in 2022, when nine child 'brides' were removed from homes. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transport a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to commit kidnapping, and on 9 December 2024 a federal judge in Phoenix sentenced him to 50 years. Two male followers who went to trial were convicted.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Focus on Children (Utah)
networks.what: Agency run by Scott and Karen Banks that arranged about 80 adoptions of Samoan children whose parents were told it was temporary schooling; the defendants pleaded guilty in January 2009 and were banned from adoption work.

networks.name: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio)
networks.what: Defunct Ohio agency that, per a 2020 federal indictment, procured more than 30 Ugandan children for US clients in 2013–2016 through bribery of Ugandan officials, and arranged a fraudulent Polish adoption. One employee pleaded guilty in 2019; others were charged in 2020.

networks.name: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho)
networks.what: Baptist group whose ten members were arrested on 29 January 2010 taking 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic; leader Laura Silsby was convicted of arranging irregular travel.

networks.name: Federal Indian boarding school system (US)
networks.what: 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or territories, 1819–1969, documented by the Department of the Interior with at least 973 child deaths and physical, sexual and emotional abuse.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.
